claim: The African turquoise killifish is a powerful vertebrate system to study complex phenotypes at scale, including aging and age-related disease.
source: The African turquoise killifish is a powerful vertebrate system to study complex phenotypes at scale, including aging and age-related disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of the model system.

claim: The killifish has a rapid timeline for sexual maturity of 3–4 weeks post hatching.
source: The African turquoise killifish Nothobranchius furzeri (hereafter killifish) has emerged as a powerful model to overcome this challenge and accelerate discovery due to its rapid timeline for sexual maturity (3–4 weeks post hatching) and naturally compressed lifespan (4–6 months) (Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu and Brunet, 2018 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: The killifish has a naturally compressed lifespan of 4–6 months.
source: The African turquoise killifish Nothobranchius furzeri (hereafter killifish) has emerged as a powerful model to overcome this challenge and accelerate discovery due to its rapid timeline for sexual maturity (3–4 weeks post hatching) and naturally compressed lifespan (4–6 months) (Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu and Brunet, 2018 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: The killifish has the shortest generation time of a vertebrate model system bred in the laboratory (2 months).
source: The killifish has the shortest generation time of a vertebrate model system bred in the laboratory (2 months) (Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Polačik et al., 2016), making rapid vertebrate genetics possible.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; and Polačik et al., 2016.

claim: A sequenced genome is available for the killifish.
source: Tools to advance genetic interrogation of the killifish have been developed, including a sequenced genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2 transgenesis (Allard et al., 2013; Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (Harel et al., 2015), and CRISPR/Cas13-mediated knock-down (Kushawah et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reichwald et al., 2015 and Valenzano et al., 2015.

claim: Tol2 transgenesis has been developed for the killifish.
source: Tools to advance genetic interrogation of the killifish have been developed, including a sequenced genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2 transgenesis (Allard et al., 2013; Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (Harel et al., 2015), and CRISPR/Cas13-mediated knock-down (Kushawah et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allard et al., 2013; Hartmann and Englert, 2012; and Valenzano et al., 2011.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out has been developed for the killifish.
source: Tools to advance genetic interrogation of the killifish have been developed, including a sequenced genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2 transgenesis (Allard et al., 2013; Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (Harel et al., 2015), and CRISPR/Cas13-mediated knock-down (Kushawah et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harel et al., 2015.

claim: CRISPR/Cas13-mediated knock-down has been developed for the killifish.
source: Tools to advance genetic interrogation of the killifish have been developed, including a sequenced genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2 transgenesis (Allard et al., 2013; Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (Harel et al., 2015), and CRISPR/Cas13-mediated knock-down (Kushawah et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kushawah et al., 2020.

claim: The genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging in killifish.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to aging studies.

claim: The genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about regeneration in killifish.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about evolution in killifish.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; and Willemsen et al., 2020.

claim: The genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about development in killifish.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abitua et al., 2021 and Dolfi et al., 2019.

claim: The genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about embryonic diapause in killifish.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2020 and Singh et al., 2021.

claim: Embryonic diapause is a state of 'suspended animation'.
source: This genetic toolkit has enabled discoveries about the mechanisms of aging (Astre et al., 2022a; Bradshaw et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Harel et al., 2022; Louka et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2017; Van Houcke et al., 2021b; Vanhunsel et al., 2021), regeneration (Vanhunsel et al., 2022a; Vanhunsel et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2020), evolution (Cui et al., 2019; Sahm et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2021; Willemsen et al., 2020), development (Abitua et al., 2021; Dolfi et al., 2019), and embryonic diapause – a state of 'suspended animation' (Hu et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated HDR is often associated with issues of low efficiency and multicopy insertion.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated HDR is often associated with issues of low efficiency and multicopy insertion (Auer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Auer et al., 2014.

claim: The dsDNA HDR template was designed with 150–200 bp homology arms flanking the site of insertion at the target locus.
source: We designed the dsDNA HDR template with 150–200 bp homology arms flanking the site of insertion at the target locus (in this case, the stop codon of a specific gene) (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The length of homology arms was selected based on IDT's recommendations for longer (>200 bp) insertions.
source: The length of homology arms was selected based on IDT's recommendations for longer (>200 bp) insertions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for the design choice.

claim: The target site for genomic insertion was designed within 2–7 bp of the Cas9 cut sites.
source: The target site for genomic insertion was designed within 2–7 bp of the Cas9 cut sites (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The T2A self-cleaving peptide avoids direct fusion of the fluorescent protein to the targeted gene's protein product.
source: Use of the T2A self-cleaving peptide avoids direct fusion of the fluorescent protein to the targeted gene's protein product (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated as the function of the T2A peptide in the design.

claim: ELAVL3 has brain-specific expression in teleost fish.
source: These three loci are known to have brain-specific (Ahrens et al., 2012), lens-specific (Posner et al., 2017), and ubiquitous (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) expression, respectively, in teleost fish (including zebrafish and medaka).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ahrens et al., 2012.

claim: CRYAA has lens-specific expression in teleost fish.
source: These three loci are known to have brain-specific (Ahrens et al., 2012), lens-specific (Posner et al., 2017), and ubiquitous (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) expression, respectively, in teleost fish (including zebrafish and medaka).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posner et al., 2017.

claim: ACTB2 has ubiquitous expression in teleost fish.
source: These three loci are known to have brain-specific (Ahrens et al., 2012), lens-specific (Posner et al., 2017), and ubiquitous (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) expression, respectively, in teleost fish (including zebrafish and medaka).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018.

claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in the developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos.
source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in the lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos.
source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos.
source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In all embryos screened, Venus expression was not observed in a tissue that was not specifically targeted.
source: In all embryos screened, we did not observe Venus expression in a tissue that was not specifically targeted.
evidence: This is a negative result reported from the screening.

claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in over 40% of developed embryos for all three targeted loci.
source: For all three targeted loci, we observed Venus fluorescence (suggestive of successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in) in over 40% of developed embryos (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The highest CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency at the ELAVL3 locus was achieved using both a chemically modified dsDNA HDR template and a small molecule HDR enhancer.
source: For the ELAVL3 locus, we achieved the highest CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency using both a chemically modified dsDNA HDR template (i.e. IDT's Alt-R HDR Donor Blocks, see Methods) and a small molecule HDR enhancer as compared to an unmodified dsDNA HDR template (i.e. IDT's gBlocks, see Methods) and no small molecule HDR enhancer (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No significant differences in lethality were observed between embryos injected with CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in reagents and non-injected wildtype embryos.
source: We did not observe significant differences in the lethality of embryos injected with CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in reagents (including chemically modified dsDNA HDR template and/or small molecule HDR enhancer) compared to non-injected wildtype embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by lethality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The lethality of killifish embryos in the first two weeks of development is variable, whether injected or not.
source: In general, the lethality of killifish embryos, whether injected or not, was variable in the first two weeks of development (dependent on breeders and clutch; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by lethality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Injecting ~100 embryos per line is recommended to ensure successful generation of transgenic animals that survive past development.
source: Thus, to ensure successful generation of transgenic animals that survive past development, we recommend injecting ~100 embryos per line.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed data.

claim: The genomic knock-in occurred at the expected genomic locus as confirmed by PCR genotyping.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that the genomic knock-in occurred at the expected genomic locus by PCR genotyping of DNA extracted from tail clips of the injected individuals (F0 founders) using 3 primers, 2 surrounding the insertion site for each gene and 1 in the Venus transgene (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 3; see below for sequencing confirmation in the F1 generation).
evidence: Supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching.
source: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching, consistent with what has been observed for ACTB2 knock-in in medaka (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) and perhaps due to the sensitivity of actin assembly to any perturbation (e.g. additional amino acids due to cleavage of the P2A peptide).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, with comparison to medaka data cited from Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018.

claim: The sensitivity of actin assembly to perturbation may explain why ACTB2 knock-in embryos did not survive hatching.
source: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching, consistent with what has been observed for ACTB2 knock-in in medaka (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) and perhaps due to the sensitivity of actin assembly to any perturbation (e.g. additional amino acids due to cleavage of the P2A peptide).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lethality.

claim: It may be more difficult to use this knock-in approach to generate stable lines targeting essential genes encoding proteins involved in sensitive assemblies such as ACTB2.
source: Hence, this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in method allows for precise and efficient editing at several loci, including tissue-specific ones; however, it may be more difficult to use this knock-in approach to generate stable lines targeting essential genes encoding proteins involved in sensitive assemblies such as ACTB2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ACTB2 lethality observation.

claim: 67% of F0 founders produced Venus-positive F1 progeny when crossed with wildtype fish.
source: Sixty-seven percent of F0 founders, when crossed with wildtype fish, produced Venus-positive F1 progeny (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by germline transmission data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: 85% of F1 Venus-positive progeny from inter-crossing two Venus-positive F0 individuals were homozygous for the insertion at the ELAVL3 locus.
source: Upon inter-crossing these founders, we found that 85% of the resulting F1 Venus-positive progeny were homozygous for the insertion at the ELAVL3 locus (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the ELAVL3 locus was single copy and in frame, with no observed mutations within 1 kb around the insertion site.
source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the ELAVL3 locus was as designed—single copy and in frame, with no observed mutations within 1 kb around the insertion site (Figure 1E; Figure 2A, C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E, Figure 2A, C, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals showed no off-target editing at the three most likely off-target sites.
source: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals at the three most likely off-target sites [predicted by CHOPCHOP (Labun et al., 2019)] showed no off-target editing at these sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Backcrossing founders to wildtype animals is recommended to limit the risk of off-target editing.
source: Nevertheless, to limit the risk of off-target editing, we recommend backcrossing founders to wildtype animals.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the potential risk of off-target editing.

claim: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord.
source: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord (Figure 2E; anti-GFP staining), which is expected given that the ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish (Ahrens et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and citation to Ahrens et al., 2012.

claim: The ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish.
source: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord (Figure 2E; anti-GFP staining), which is expected given that the ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish (Ahrens et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ahrens et al., 2012.

claim: In adults, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F3 heterozygous individuals show strong Venus expression in the brain.
source: In adults, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F3 heterozygous individuals show strong Venus expression in the brain (Figure 2F) (while we did not specifically test retina and spinal cord in adults, Venus expression should also occur in these areas).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Venus transcript colocalizes to the same brain regions and cells as the ELAVL3 transcript in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line.
source: In situ hybridization indicates that the Venus transcript indeed colocalizes to the same brain regions and cells as the ELAVL3 transcript (Figure 2F; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The ELAVL3 transcript expression pattern in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line is consistent with that of ELAVL3 in wildtype animals.
source: The ELAVL3 transcript expression pattern in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line is consistent with that of ELAVL3 in wildtype animals (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2G.

claim: The knocked-in Venus transgene recapitulates the endogenous expression pattern of the targeted ELAVL3 locus in the brain.
source: Together, these results suggest that the knocked-in Venus transgene recapitulates the endogenous expression pattern of the targeted ELAVL3 locus in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: A large increase in expression of Venus was observed in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals.
source: As expected, we observed a large increase in expression of Venus in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals (with highest expression of Venus in homozygous animals; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: ELAVL3 expression level was not significantly different between animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype siblings.
source: ELAVL3 expression level was not significantly different between animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype siblings (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; although there might be a slight, non-significant reduction in the homozygous mutants).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Inserting a fluorescent protein gene at the endogenous ELAVL3 locus does not significantly impair the expression of the endogenous gene.
source: Thus, inserting a fluorescent protein gene at the endogenous ELAVL3 locus does not significantly impair the expression of the endogenous gene.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RT-qPCR data.

claim: The knock-in method enables generation of stable lines of transgenic vertebrate animals in 2–3 months.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that the knock-in method we developed enables generation of stable lines of transgenic vertebrate animals in 2–3 months.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the timeline of the experiments.

claim: Successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of a 2 kb long insertion sequence was observed in ~50% of developed embryos.
source: We observed successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of this longer sequence in ~50% of developed embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by efficiency data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was no decrease in efficiency or change in embryo lethality for the 2 kb insertion relative to the shorter 0.8 kb insertion at the ELAVL3 locus.
source: There was no decrease in efficiency or change in embryo lethality for this longer insertion relative to the shorter (0.8 kb) insertion previously tested at the same locus (Figure 3B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet integration at the ELAVL3 locus was the expected size and in frame without mutations.
source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet integration at the ELAVL3 locus was the expected size and in frame without mutations (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet animals showed no off-target editing at the three predicted most likely off-target sites.
source: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals at the three predicted most likely off-target sites showed no off-target editing in these fish (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Imaging coronal brain sections of adult F0 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish showed cells expressing both oScarlet and Venus.
source: Imaging coronal brain sections of adult F0 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish showed cells expressing both oScarlet and Venus (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: oScarlet expression was confined to nuclei while Venus expression was seen in both cell bodies and projections in ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish.
source: As expected, oScarlet expression was confined to nuclei while Venus expression was seen in both cell bodies and projections (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Imaging the whole brain of adult ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish revealed oScarlet-positive nuclei throughout the brain.
source: Imaging the whole brain of adult ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish revealed oScarlet-positive nuclei throughout the brain (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: This method allows for pan-neuronal expression in the adult brain and could be leveraged to drive expression of molecular tools in a neuronal-specific manner.
source: Thus, this method allows for pan-neuronal expression in the adult brain and could be leveraged to drive expression of molecular tools e.g. the optogenetic ion channel channelrhodopsin [~1 kb] (Boyden et al., 2005) or the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP [~1.3 kb] (Ahrens et al., 2012) in a neuronal-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference about potential applications based on the demonstrated capability.

claim: NPY and HCRT neuronal populations are critical for organismal homeostasis through modulation of behaviors, including feeding behavior and sleep-wake behavior.
source: These neuronal populations are critical for organismal homeostasis through modulation of behaviors, including feeding behavior (Jeong et al., 2018) and sleep-wake behavior (Chiu and Prober, 2013; Prober et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeong et al., 2018; Chiu and Prober, 2013; Prober et al., 2006; and Singh et al., 2017.

claim: Growing evidence suggests that NPY and HCRT neuronal populations may be altered with age.
source: Growing evidence also suggests that these neuronal populations may be altered with age (Fronczek et al., 2012; Hunt et al., 2015; Li et al., 2022; Montesano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fronczek et al., 2012; Hunt et al., 2015; Li et al., 2022; and Montesano et al., 2019.

claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the NPY or HCRT locus was single-copy and in frame at the targeted genomic location.
source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the NPY or HCRT locus was as designed—single-copy and in frame at the targeted genomic location (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Imaging of coronal brain sections of the adult HCRT-T2A-Venus killifish line showed a dense and isolated population of Venus-positive cell bodies in the dorsal periventricular hypothalamus.
source: Imaging of coronal brain sections of the adult HCRT-T2A-Venus killifish line showed a dense and isolated population of Venus-positive cell bodies in the dorsal periventricular hypothalamus (Hd; homologous to the mammalian arcuate nucleus; Figure 4B), consistent with endogenous HCRT expression previously reported in the adult killifish brain (D'angelo, 2013; Montesano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and citations to D'angelo, 2013 and Montesano et al., 2019.

claim: The adult NPY-T2A-Venus line exhibited Venus-positive cell bodies throughout the brain, including in the central posterior thalamic nucleus, anterior tuberal nucleus, periventricular and lateral hypothalamus, and periventricular gray zone of the optic tectum.
source: In contrast, the adult NPY-T2A-Venus line exhibited Venus-positive cell bodies throughout the brain, including in the central posterior thalamic nucleus (CP), anterior tuberal nucleus (TNa), periventricular and lateral hypothalamus, as well as in the periventricular gray zone (PGZ) of the optic tectum (OT) (Figure 4D), consistent with endogenous NPY expression previously reported in the adult killifish brain (D'angelo, 2013; Montesano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D and citations to D'angelo, 2013 and Montesano et al., 2019.

claim: Venus transcript co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line.
source: Using in situ hybridization, we verified that Venus transcript indeed co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5) or the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Venus transcript co-localized with the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line.
source: Using in situ hybridization, we verified that Venus transcript indeed co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5) or the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Venus expression profiles observed in the NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines were consistent with those of endogenous NPY and HCRT transcripts, respectively, in wildtype animals.
source: The Venus expression profiles observed in the NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines were consistent with those of endogenous NPY and HCRT transcripts, respectively, in wildtype animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A large increase in expression of Venus was observed in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals.
source: As expected, we observed a large increase in expression of Venus in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals (with highest expression of Venus in homozygous animals; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: In animals heterozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was similar to that of wildtype animals.
source: In animals heterozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was similar to that of wildtype animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: In animals homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was slightly but significantly lower compared to wildtype siblings.
source: However, in animals homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was slightly but significantly lower compared to wildtype siblings (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of the transgene at homozygous levels slightly impairs expression of endogenous NPY.
source: These observations suggest that the presence of the transgene at homozygous levels slightly impairs expression of endogenous NPY.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RT-qPCR data.

claim: Use of heterozygous animals with edited alleles may be more conservative to preserve robust expression of the endogenous locus.
source: Thus, in this case (and likely in other cases), use of heterozygous animals with edited alleles may be more conservative to preserve robust expression of the endogenous locus.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the NPY expression data.

claim: The observation that the expression pattern of Venus recapitulates that of the targeted endogenous gene for all genes targeted supports the notion that in-frame off-target insertions are rare with this method.
source: The observation that the expression pattern of Venus recapitulates that of the targeted endogenous gene for all genes targeted here also supports the notion that in-frame off-target insertions are rare with this method.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern data.

claim: The generation of NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines serves as proof of principle that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in is a powerful method in killifish to drive cell-type-specific expression.
source: The generation of these lines serves as proof of principle that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in is a powerful method in killifish to drive cell-type-specific expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful generation of cell-type-specific lines.

claim: These neuron-specific lines should help the development of the killifish for systems neuroscience studies.
source: These neuron-specific lines should also help the development of the killifish for systems neuroscience studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of large inserts was observed at five distinct genomic loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, ACTB2, NPY, and HCRT), with >40% efficiency at tested loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, and ACTB2).
source: We observe CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of large inserts at five distinct genomic loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, ACTB2, NPY, and HCRT), with >40% efficiency at tested loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, and ACTB2).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: With this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach, a >65% germline transmission rate was observed for knock-in at the ELAVL3 locus.
source: With this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach, we observe a >65% germline transmission rate for knock-in at the ELAVL3 locus.
evidence: This is a summary of the germline transmission data.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency and germline transmission rates may vary depending on the genomic locus being targeted.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency and germline transmission rates may vary depending on the genomic locus being targeted (Hsu et al., 2013; Labun et al., 2019), which might be due to the chromatin accessibility of that locus.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2013 and Labun et al., 2019.

claim: Four stable knock-in lines were generated in this work: ELAVL3-T2A-Venus, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet, NPY-T2A-Venus, and HCRT-T2A-Venus.
source: We have generated four stable knock-in lines in this work: ELAVL3-T2A-Venus, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet, NPY-T2A-Venus, and HCRT-T2A-Venus.
evidence: This is a summary of the lines generated.

claim: The high efficiency of germline transmission observed in killifish may be due to the relatively slow rate of early cell division after fertilization in the African turquoise killifish.
source: The high efficiency of germline transmission we observe in killifish may be due to the relatively slow rate of early cell division after fertilization in the African turquoise killifish (~4 times slower in this species relative to non-annual teleost fishes; Dolfi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Dolfi et al., 2014.

claim: The killifish model allows for easy and high-throughput injection of genome-editing machinery into embryos.
source: The killifish model, with hundreds of embryos produced at a given time (for example using harem breeding), allows for easy and high-throughput injection of genome-editing machinery into embryos (Harel et al., 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Polačik et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harel et al., 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; and Polačik et al., 2016.

claim: The development of rapid and efficient knock-in establishes the killifish as a system for precise genetic engineering at scale.
source: The development of rapid and efficient knock-in establishes the killifish as a system for precise genetic engineering at scale, which has been challenging so far in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: Knock-in was first reported for short insertions (~8 bp) in killifish, though germline transmission of these inserts was not achieved.
source: Knock-in was first reported for short insertions (~8 bp; though germline transmission of these inserts was not achieved) (Harel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harel et al., 2015.

claim: Longer CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in insertions (~1 kb) were achieved in killifish (in F0 individuals) with 18–30% efficiency, though germline transmission was not shown.
source: More recently, longer CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in insertions (~1 kb) were achieved in killifish (in F0 individuals) with 18–30% efficiency, though germline transmission was not shown (Oginuma et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oginuma et al., 2022.

claim: Knock-in of a long (1.5 kb) insertion was achieved for a specific locus with ~11% efficiency and successful germline transmission.
source: Moreover, knock-in of a long (1.5 kb) insertion was achieved for a specific locus with ~11% efficiency and successful germline transmission (germline transmission rate not shown) (Krug et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krug et al., 2023.

claim: The knock-in method developed here uses reagents that are commercially available, eliminating the need for cloning and PCR.
source: The knock-in method developed here uses reagents that are commercially available, eliminating the need for cloning and PCR and making this method easy to adopt.
evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claim: The steps described here could serve as a blueprint for knock-in approaches in other emerging model organisms.
source: Together, the steps described here could serve as a blueprint for knock-in approaches in other emerging model organisms.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader applications.

claim: High insertion efficiencies (>40%) and germline transmission have been achieved with different CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in methods in teleost fish.
source: While it is difficult without side-by-side experiments to compare each knock-in approach, high insertion efficiencies (>40%) and germline transmission have been achieved with different methods, for example, in zebrafish using plasmid donors with in vivo linearization and short homology arms (Wierson et al., 2020), in medaka using dsDNA PCR product donors, biotin modification and short homology arms (Seleit et al., 2021), and (reported here) in killifish using synthetic dsDNA donors, IDT's proprietary modification (Alt-R HDR Donor Block) and middle-range length (150–200 bp) homology arms.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wierson et al., 2020 and Seleit et al., 2021, and data from this study.

claim: A variety of approaches for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in have been successful in teleost fish, expanding the toolkit that can be used in these species.
source: Thus, a variety of approaches for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in have been successful in teleost fish, expanding the toolkit that can be used in these species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different methods.

claim: The use of synthetic, chemically-modified repair templates with ~150–200 bp homology arms has the advantage of being easily adoptable without expertise in molecular biology techniques.
source: Our method uses synthetic, chemically-modified repair templates with ~150–200 bp homology arms, which has the advantage of being easily adoptable without expertise in molecular biology techniques (cloning or PCR).
evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claim: There is no preparation required for reagents in this method, which helps save hands-on time.
source: In addition, there is no preparation required for reagents (e.g. cloning or amplification with cleanup steps), which helps save hands-on time.
evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claim: The use of synthetic reagents that are sequenced and quality-controlled reduces the likelihood of mutations in the HDR template.
source: Finally, the use of synthetic reagents that are sequenced and quality-controlled reduces the likelihood of mutations in the HDR template.
evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claim: The use of synthetic HDR templates has limitations including a limit on the total length (≤3000 bp) and complexity of dsDNA HDR templates that can be synthesized.
source: However, the use of synthetic HDR templates does have limitations: (1) there is a limit on the total length (≤3000 bp) and complexity of dsDNA HDR templates that can be synthesized (e.g. sequence containing repetitive elements), (2) there is a wait time to receive the synthesized template, and (3) synthesis of large templates can be expensive.
evidence: This is a description of the method's limitations.

claim: If generating a few CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in lines, a purely synthetic approach would likely require the least amount of hands-on work and start-up time.
source: If generating a few CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in lines, a purely synthetic approach would likely require the least amount of hands-on work and start-up time.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on practical considerations.

claim: If planning to design many lines, a modular cloning/PCR based approach may be most cost effective.
source: In contrast, if one is planning to design many lines, a modular cloning/PCR based approach may be most cost effective.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on practical considerations.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach should allow the establishment of versatile strategies to probe complex phenotypes, including development, 'suspended animation' (embryonic diapause), regeneration, aging, and age-related diseases.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach we developed should allow the establishment of versatile strategies to probe complex phenotypes, including development, 'suspended animation' (embryonic diapause), regeneration, aging, and age-related diseases.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: This knock-in method should allow the generation of human disease models that can be studied longitudinally, over an entire lifespan.
source: Given the potential of the African killifish for modeling human aging (Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Van Houcke et al., 2021a), this knock-in method should also allow the generation of human disease models that can be studied longitudinally, over an entire lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications, supported by citations to Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; and Van Houcke et al., 2021a.

claim: Human disease variant models in mice have been critical to understand disease mechanisms and treatment strategies.
source: Human disease variant models in mice have been critical to understand disease mechanisms and treatment strategies (Dawson et al., 2018; Fisher and Bannerman, 2019; Jankowsky and Zheng, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2018; Fisher and Bannerman, 2019; and Jankowsky and Zheng, 2017.

claim: Generating human disease models that are scalable and integrate both genetics and age as risk factors has the potential to identify new strategies to treat these diseases.
source: Generating human disease models that are scalable and integrate both genetics and age as risk factors has the potential to identify new strategies to treat these diseases.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential impact of the method.

claim: This study highlights the power of knock-in, combined with self-cleaving peptides, to drive cell-type-specific expression of ectopic genes.
source: This study highlights the power of knock-in, combined with self-cleaving peptides, to drive cell-type-specific expression of ectopic genes such as molecular reporters (e.g. fluorescent reporters, calcium indicators), recombinases (e.g. Cre), and optogenetic tools (e.g. light sensitive ion channels such as channelrhodopsin).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: The cell-type resolution of this genetic tool should open studies in a variety of fields, including systems neuroscience.
source: The cell-type resolution of this genetic tool should open studies in a variety of fields, including systems neuroscience.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: Additional variations, such as the use of 'landing pads' and inducible promoters, could be further developed to complete this toolkit.
source: Additional variations, such as the use of 'landing pads' (i.e. genetic loci that support stable long-term expression of transgenes such as ROSA26 in mice; Soriano, 1999) and inducible promoters (either endogenous or ectopic; Gossen and Bujard, 1992; Gossen et al., 1995), could be further developed to complete this toolkit.
evidence: This is a speculation about future developments, supported by citations to Soriano, 1999; Gossen and Bujard, 1992; and Gossen et al., 1995.

claim: This knock-in method should accelerate the use of the killifish as a scalable vertebrate model and allow discoveries in several fields, including regeneration, neuroscience, aging, and disease, with conserved implications for humans.
source: Overall, this knock-in method should accelerate the use of the killifish as a scalable vertebrate model and allow discoveries in several fields, including regeneration, neuroscience, aging, and disease, with conserved implications for humans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader impact of the method.

claim: African turquoise killifish (GRZ strain) were maintained at 26–27 °C in a central filtration recirculating system.
source: African turquoise killifish (GRZ strain) were maintained according to established guidelines (Astre et al., 2022b; Bedbrook et al., 2023; Nath et al., 2023; Reichard et al., 2022; Žák et al., 2020). Briefly, animals were housed at 26–27 °C in a central filtration recirculating system (Aquaneering, San Diego) at a conductivity between 3800–4000 μS/cm and a pH between 6.5–7.0, with a daily exchange of 10% water treated by reverse osmosis (i.e. RO water).
evidence: This is a description of the husbandry methods.

claim: Animals were kept on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and were fed twice a day on weekdays and once a day on weekends.
source: Animals were kept on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and were fed twice a day on weekdays and once a day on weekends.
evidence: This is a description of the husbandry methods.

claim: Adult fish (>1 month of age) were fed dry fish food while young fish (<1 month of age) were fed freshly hatched brine shrimp.
source: Adult fish (>1 month of age) were fed dry fish food (Otohime fish diet, Reed Mariculture, Otohime C1) while young fish (<1 month of age) were fed freshly hatched brine shrimp (Brine Shrimp Direct, BSEP6LB).
evidence: This is a description of the husbandry methods.
